A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FragFM framework and NPGen benchmark. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–F support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: V3 reports original molecular-generation benchmarks, conditional-generation experiments, reconstruction tests, and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: V4 retains these original experiments and adds baseline evaluations, fragmentation and decoder ablations, retrosynthetic analysis, and embedding and diversity analyses.

M1.justification: The autoencoder, Blossom decoding, stochastic fragment bags, joint discrete/continuous flows, and dual guidance remain the same. Newly explicit regressor objectives document existing components. Equation 30 repairs the retained Gaussian-guidance derivation; the PDFs do not establish an underlying algorithm change.

E1.justification: Both versions use MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, and NPGen, with the same molecular-property and protein-docking targets. New retrosynthesis, fragmentation, diversity, and embedding analyses examine retained molecular populations rather than introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V4 adds MolHF and MolGrow to MOSES Table 1; SAFE-GPT, MolHF, and DeFoG to NPGen Table 2; and MolHF to ZINC250k Table 5. SAFE-GPT and DeFoG already appeared elsewhere in v3, but their NPGen participation is new. These additions substantially broaden the relevant comparison families.

E3.justification: V4 extends evaluation with a 25,000-molecule AiZynthFinder protocol measuring solved routes and reaction steps, internal-diversity measurement, and fragmentation/decoder controls. Appendix B.2 corrects the stated split from 85:5:15 to 80:5:15 while retaining identical counts. Appendix A.4 changes reported GuacaMol/NPGen node/edge stochasticity parameters from (10,2) to (2,20). These revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V4 adds RECAP/rBRICS fragmentation ablations (Section 5.5), retrosynthetic accessibility analysis (C.2), random-decoder inference ablation (C.3), guidance-versus-diversity analysis (C.8), and learned-fragment embedding analysis (F.2). These test additional robustness, component-role, and chemical-organization questions. V3's random-latent, fragment-generalization, long-tail, bag-size, and temperature analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V3 Table 5 and v4 Table 6 both report NPGen means and standard deviations over three runs. Added baseline rows follow that existing practice. Three-run averaging elsewhere is retained, without new confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Existing FragFM benchmark scores remain, but substantial results are added. In NPGen Table 2, new SAFE-GPT results give FCD 0.15 versus FragFM's retained 1.34, with novelty 73.5% versus 95.4%, changing the distributional ranking. New Table 9 reports FCD 0.90 with a random decoder versus 0.58 normally. V4 also removes the extra 500-step DiGress row reporting 84.8% validity and FCD 1.37 from v3 Table 11.

T1.justification: Equation 30 changes all three guidance exponents from positive to negative squared-error gradients, restoring consistency with the preceding Gaussian-likelihood derivation. The flow, diffusion-bridge, and detailed-balance mathematics otherwise remains intact. New Equations 35–36 explicitly document objectives for the existing property regressors.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims about FragFM's hierarchical framework, scalable fragment bags, NPGen, sampling efficiency, and property control. The added evidence does not redefine those stated contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 qualifies NPGen superiority to graph-based models and acknowledges SAFE-GPT's stronger distributional alignment but lower novelty. V4 also adds interpretations concerning decoder fidelity, synthesis-oriented fragment bias, chemically organized embeddings, and the modest diversity cost of stronger guidance. Existing novelty and scaffold-vocabulary limitations remain.

D1.justification: V4 adds a code/data availability statement and repository link, NPGen baseline training recipes, explicit jointly trained property-regression objectives, and labeled-data-use disclosure. Table 16 corrects swapped loss-weight labels to fragment type 1 and edge 5, matching Equation 25 already in v3, and clarifies 384 as the fragment bag size.

R1.justification: New Section 2.3 positions FragFM against MolGrow, MolHF, and hierarchical 3D generation, distinguishing chemically defined fragments from implicit graph coarsening. References also add fragment-generation, AiZynthFinder, RECAP, and rBRICS works. The broader positioning remains intact; DiGress's 2022-to-2023 citation change updates the same work.

P1.justification: V4 retains the main section sequence and most prose while adding focused subsections, rewriting the NPGen results discussion, and correcting language and terminology. It also revises author/affiliation formatting and adds conference headers and acknowledgments. The narrative is extended rather than substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: V4 adds ablation Tables 3 and 9, retrosynthesis Figure 10, diversity Figure 20, and embedding Figures 25–27. Benchmark tables expand with comparator rows and graph/sequence labels, and ZINC250k metric-direction arrows are corrected. Existing plots and molecular examples are also resized or relocated. These changes substantially expand the visual evidence beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens empirical credibility. The expanded NPGen comparison exposes SAFE-GPT's fidelity/novelty tradeoff and supports a more qualified interpretation. New fragmentation and decoder controls, retrosynthetic evaluation, and diversity analysis address important gaps in validating the proposed design and its practical tradeoffs. Mathematical and reporting corrections improve reproducibility. Although retrosynthesis remains a computational proxy and core scores are unchanged, the conclusions are materially better tested and calibrated.
